PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
CON
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.

### Prepared by the Attorney General
## Healthcare Insurance. Rate Changes. Initiative Statute.
- Requires changes to health insurance rates, or anything else affecting the charges associated with health insurance, to be approved by Insurance Commissioner before taking effect.
- Provides for public notice, disclosure, and hearing on health insurance rate changes, and subsequent judicial review.
- Requires sworn statement by health insurer as to accuracy of information submitted to Insurance Commissioner to justify rate changes.
- Does not apply to employer large group health plans.
- Prohibits health, auto, and homeowners insurers from determining policy eligibility or rates based on lack of prior coverage or credit history.
### Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact:
- Increased state administrative costs to regulate health insurance, likely not exceeding the low millions of dollars annually in most years, funded from fees paid by health insurance companies.

## California Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber, Ph.D., Announces the Statewide Voter Information Guide for the November 3, 2026, General Election Is Available for Public Review
**Sacramento, Calif.** – Today California Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber, Ph.D., made the November 3, 2026, California General Election Official Voter Information Guide available for public review.
The guide, which will be mailed to every voting household in California, includes information about propositions and statements from candidates running for constitutional offices, as well as other important election information such as the California Voter Bill of Rights and information about how eligible Californians can vote.
California’s Official Voter Information Guide is available in 10 languages—English, Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, Japanese, Khmer, Korean, Tagalog, Thai, and Vietnamese.
The guide is available for public examination from July 21, 2026 through August 10, 2026 at https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/public-display and at the Office of the Secretary of State’s Sacramento and Los Angeles locations.
...
Following the conclusion of the public examination period, the Office of the Secretary of State will begin printing and mailing the statewide Voter Information Guide to all households that have at least one registered voter.

Secretary Weber also invited interested Californians to submit arguments to be considered for inclusion in the Official Voter Information Guide.
The guide is mailed to every voting household in California and posted on the Secretary of State’s website.

PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
CON
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.

- Provides for public notice, disclosure, and hearing on health insurance rate changes, and subsequent judicial review.
- Requires sworn statement by health insurer as to accuracy of information submitted to Insurance Commissioner to justify rate changes.
- Does not apply to employer large group health plans.
- Prohibits health, auto, and homeowners insurers from determining policy eligibility or rates based on lack of prior coverage or credit history.

PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
CON
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.

Prop 45’s final weekend: two polls, two different answers, and a Bay Area that is the measure’s toughest crowd
PPIC’s October survey has the CEQA overhaul trailing 46% to 50% among likely voters, down from a narrow lead in September. A Probolsky Research poll has it narrowly ahead. Probolsky finds the Bay Area the most skeptical region.
November 1, 2026
Top image: The California State Capitol in Sacramento. Photo: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:California_State_Capitol_from_Capitol_Mall_-_Sacramento_(26429122855).jpg)
By Gideon Paley (https://southbaychronicle.com/reporters/#gideon-paley), Real Estate Development Reporter
ANALYSIS | What the late polling shows on the CEQA overhaul
Prop 45 heads into the last weekend before Tuesday’s election as a close race in the polls. The measure would put deadlines on environmental review and lawsuits under the California Environmental Quality Act for housing, water, energy and other projects it defines as essential.
PPIC: behind, and slipping
The Public Policy Institute of California’s October statewide survey, taken Oct. 16-22, found 46% of likely voters would vote yes, 50% no and 4% undecided, according to PPIC (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/). In September the same survey had the measure ahead, 49% to 46%. The October likely-voter sample was 1,086, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points, so the race is within that range.
The partisan split runs the opposite way from many California housing fights. A majority of Republicans support the measure, while 54% of Democrats oppose it, PPIC found. Gov. Gavin Newsom has stayed on the sidelines, The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) reported. PPIC also measured Prop 40 at 46% yes and 52% no.
Housing under construction at San Francisco’s former Upper Yard site in May 2022. Photo: Pi.1415926535 / CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Upper_Yard_housing_construction,_May_2022.jpg)
Probolsky: ahead, barely
A Probolsky Research poll released Oct. 27 points the other way. The firm headlined its findings “Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/2026/10/27/yes-on-prop-45-leads-by-a-thin-margin/).” It has not published full toplines, and it says it has no client in the race. Men back the measure 51% to 36%, while women oppose it 42% to 36%, the firm reported.
Probolsky also found the Bay Area to be the measure’s weakest region. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up,” Probolsky said in its release.
The money
Both sides are spending heavily. Filings with the Fair Political Practices Commission as of Oct. 29 showed about $39.6 million raised for the Yes side and about $36.3 million for the No side. The Chronicle’s analysis of who is funding each side (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/31/analysis-who-is-funding-prop-45-and-why/) breaks down the largest donors.
Transmission lines carry power from the Encina Power Plant in Carlsbad. Prop. 45 would also cover energy and water projects, not only housing. Photo: Chris Hunkeler from Carlsbad, California, USA / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Transmission_Lines_(8550788014).jpg)
What supporters and opponents argue
Supporters say CEQA lawsuits and open-ended reviews have become a main cause of delay and cost for new housing and infrastructure, and that firm deadlines would get projects built faster. Opponents, including environmental and some labor groups, say the measure would weaken a key tool communities use to challenge harmful projects. The Chronicle’s editorial board has recommended a No vote (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/25/editorial-vote-no-on-prop-45/). That editorial is separate from this newsroom’s reporting.
What to watch Tuesday
The two polls together suggest the result could come down to turnout, especially among Democrats who are splitting from their usual allies and among Bay Area voters. Many California mail ballots are counted after Election Day, so a close statewide measure may not be called on election night.

Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin
October 27, 2026 / in News, Insights & Research (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/category/news-insight-and-research/) / by Probolsky Research (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/author/probolsky-research/)
Probolsky Research regularly conducts election and public policy polling for public interest. We have released these results for California Proposition 45 on the November ballot for public interest . The company has no client in the race nor any affiliation with the respective campaigns.
“There is a clear gender divide on Prop. 45. Men support the measure 51% to 36%. Women oppose it 42% to 36%,” explained Dr. Adam Probolsky, president of Probolsky Research. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up.”

By Gideon Paley (https://southbaychronicle.com/reporters/#gideon-paley), Real Estate Development Reporter
ANALYSIS | What the late polling shows on the CEQA overhaul
Prop 45 heads into the last weekend before Tuesday’s election as a close race in the polls. The measure would put deadlines on environmental review and lawsuits under the California Environmental Quality Act for housing, water, energy and other projects it defines as essential.
PPIC: behind, and slipping
The Public Policy Institute of California’s October statewide survey, taken Oct. 16-22, found 46% of likely voters would vote yes, 50% no and 4% undecided, according to PPIC (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/). In September the same survey had the measure ahead, 49% to 46%. The October likely-voter sample was 1,086, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points, so the race is within that range.
The partisan split runs the opposite way from many California housing fights. A majority of Republicans support the measure, while 54% of Democrats oppose it, PPIC found. Gov. Gavin Newsom has stayed on the sidelines, The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) reported. PPIC also measured Prop 40 at 46% yes and 52% no.
Housing under construction at San Francisco’s former Upper Yard site in May 2022. Photo: Pi.1415926535 / CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Upper_Yard_housing_construction,_May_2022.jpg)
Probolsky: ahead, barely
A Probolsky Research poll released Oct. 27 points the other way. The firm headlined its findings “Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/2026/10/27/yes-on-prop-45-leads-by-a-thin-margin/).” It has not published full toplines, and it says it has no client in the race. Men back the measure 51% to 36%, while women oppose it 42% to 36%, the firm reported.
Probolsky also found the Bay Area to be the measure’s weakest region. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up,” Probolsky said in its release.
The money
Both sides are spending heavily. Filings with the Fair Political Practices Commission as of Oct. 29 showed about $39.6 million raised for the Yes side and about $36.3 million for the No side. The Chronicle’s analysis of who is funding each side (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/31/analysis-who-is-funding-prop-45-and-why/) breaks down the largest donors.
Transmission lines carry power from the Encina Power Plant in Carlsbad. Prop. 45 would also cover energy and water projects, not only housing. Photo: Chris Hunkeler from Carlsbad, California, USA / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Transmission_Lines_(8550788014).jpg)
What supporters and opponents argue
Supporters say CEQA lawsuits and open-ended reviews have become a main cause of delay and cost for new housing and infrastructure, and that firm deadlines would get projects built faster. Opponents, including environmental and some labor groups, say the measure would weaken a key tool communities use to challenge harmful projects. The Chronicle’s editorial board has recommended a No vote (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/25/editorial-vote-no-on-prop-45/). That editorial is separate from this newsroom’s reporting.
What to watch Tuesday
The two polls together suggest the result could come down to turnout, especially among Democrats who are splitting from their usual allies and among Bay Area voters. Many California mail ballots are counted after Election Day, so a close statewide measure may not be called on election night.

Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin
October 27, 2026 / in News, Insights & Research (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/category/news-insight-and-research/) / by Probolsky Research (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/author/probolsky-research/)
Probolsky Research regularly conducts election and public policy polling for public interest. We have released these results for California Proposition 45 on the November ballot for public interest . The company has no client in the race nor any affiliation with the respective campaigns.
“There is a clear gender divide on Prop. 45. Men support the measure 51% to 36%. Women oppose it 42% to 36%,” explained Dr. Adam Probolsky, president of Probolsky Research. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up.”

Prop 45’s final weekend: two polls, two different answers, and a Bay Area that is the measure’s toughest crowd
PPIC’s October survey has the CEQA overhaul trailing 46% to 50% among likely voters, down from a narrow lead in September. A Probolsky Research poll has it narrowly ahead. Probolsky finds the Bay Area the most skeptical region.
November 1, 2026
Top image: The California State Capitol in Sacramento. Photo: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:California_State_Capitol_from_Capitol_Mall_-_Sacramento_(26429122855).jpg)
By Gideon Paley (https://southbaychronicle.com/reporters/#gideon-paley), Real Estate Development Reporter
ANALYSIS | What the late polling shows on the CEQA overhaul
Prop 45 heads into the last weekend before Tuesday’s election as a close race in the polls. The measure would put deadlines on environmental review and lawsuits under the California Environmental Quality Act for housing, water, energy and other projects it defines as essential.
PPIC: behind, and slipping
The Public Policy Institute of California’s October statewide survey, taken Oct. 16-22, found 46% of likely voters would vote yes, 50% no and 4% undecided, according to PPIC (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/). In September the same survey had the measure ahead, 49% to 46%. The October likely-voter sample was 1,086, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points, so the race is within that range.
The partisan split runs the opposite way from many California housing fights. A majority of Republicans support the measure, while 54% of Democrats oppose it, PPIC found. Gov. Gavin Newsom has stayed on the sidelines, The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) reported. PPIC also measured Prop 40 at 46% yes and 52% no.
Housing under construction at San Francisco’s former Upper Yard site in May 2022. Photo: Pi.1415926535 / CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Upper_Yard_housing_construction,_May_2022.jpg)
Probolsky: ahead, barely
A Probolsky Research poll released Oct. 27 points the other way. The firm headlined its findings “Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/2026/10/27/yes-on-prop-45-leads-by-a-thin-margin/).” It has not published full toplines, and it says it has no client in the race. Men back the measure 51% to 36%, while women oppose it 42% to 36%, the firm reported.
Probolsky also found the Bay Area to be the measure’s weakest region. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up,” Probolsky said in its release.
The money
Both sides are spending heavily. Filings with the Fair Political Practices Commission as of Oct. 29 showed about $39.6 million raised for the Yes side and about $36.3 million for the No side. The Chronicle’s analysis of who is funding each side (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/31/analysis-who-is-funding-prop-45-and-why/) breaks down the largest donors.
Transmission lines carry power from the Encina Power Plant in Carlsbad. Prop. 45 would also cover energy and water projects, not only housing. Photo: Chris Hunkeler from Carlsbad, California, USA / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Transmission_Lines_(8550788014).jpg)
What supporters and opponents argue
Supporters say CEQA lawsuits and open-ended reviews have become a main cause of delay and cost for new housing and infrastructure, and that firm deadlines would get projects built faster. Opponents, including environmental and some labor groups, say the measure would weaken a key tool communities use to challenge harmful projects. The Chronicle’s editorial board has recommended a No vote (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/25/editorial-vote-no-on-prop-45/). That editorial is separate from this newsroom’s reporting.
What to watch Tuesday
The two polls together suggest the result could come down to turnout, especially among Democrats who are splitting from their usual allies and among Bay Area voters. Many California mail ballots are counted after Election Day, so a close statewide measure may not be called on election night.

Proposition 45 is forecast as a environment and energy measure whose Yes vote leans to neither party . The picture: as of Nov 2, 2026, the best evidence says No leads slightly (PPIC 50-46), with a single low-transparency poll (Probolsky) showing Yes narrowly ahead. The forecast model says No has 52.3% chance.

Additional structural factors favoring No:
- Strong Democratic environment in 2026 CA midterm (Becerra +27, Dem enthusiasm).
- State Democratic Party opposed; major unions? Let's check labor: opponents led by coalition of 550 labor, health, environmental orgs. Yes side includes some labor (building trades?). Let me check whether the State Building and Construction Trades Council supported it. That matters: if labor is split, Democratic voters get mixed cues.
- Many progressive Dems and environmentalists opposed; data center controversy is a potent attack.
- 41-page complex measure; confusion → No.

Factors favoring Yes:
- Massive spending ($56M spent vs $30M), 28 newspaper endorsements, business/labor coalition, affordability messaging salient (cost of living top issue).
- Base support for CEQA reform concept is very high (73% with generic description).
- Republicans mostly support; also independent-leaning YIMBYs.
- In California, "Yes" votes on pro-housing/infrastructure measures often outperform polls.

Historical analogies: Prop 1 (2024 water bond) passed 50.6% despite polling close. Prop 30 (2022, tax for EVs) failed despite big spending. Prop 22 (2020) passed despite opposition. Prop 23, Prop 25 (2020)... Hmm.

Consider also that measures with big financial advantages and broad coalition support in CA often overperform. But the key metric here: PPIC's likely-voter poll with ballot language at 46-50, 4% undecided. Historically, when PPIC's final poll shows a measure below 50% with small undecided, the measure usually fails.

Now, the money is roughly balanced: Yes ~$38-41M, No ~$31-38M. Notably, the No side got large late contributions ($5.3M late from Campaign for People Over Polluters). So money advantage for Yes is not overwhelming.

Key: PPIC October (most recent reputable poll, using official ballot language, LV): No 50, Yes 46, 4% DK. Probolsky Oct 27 (thin Yes lead, no toplines). Forecast: No 52.3%.

Structural considerations that push toward No:
1. California's electorate in 2026 midterms: heavily Democratic (Becerra +27), and 54% of Democrats oppose, majority of Republicans support. Democratic turnout advantage in a midterm where Democrats are motivated against Trump. This is a meaningful headwind.
2. The measure's support collapsed once the specifics/attacks (data centers, oil, corporate funders, gutting CEQA) landed. Momentum against.
3. Complexity: 41 pages, initiative statute; hard to explain. Undecided voters default to No on complex measures.
4. The "Yes" campaign lacks Democratic elite support: Newsom neutral, Becerra neutral, Wiener neutral, California YIMBY neutral, building trades opposed, state Democratic Party opposed.
5. Historical base rates: California initiative statutes pass at roughly 40%; measures polling below 50% in final polls rarely pass. Also, measures opposed by labor + environmentalists in a Dem year tend to fail.
6. Also: measures that are "status quo" default (No = keep existing law) with attack ads framing them as corporate giveaways.

Structural considerations for Yes:
1. Big business coalition, utilities, homebuilders; strong affordability message that resonates (cost of living top issue for many).
2. Conceptual support for CEQA reform is very high (73% generic).
3. Newspaper endorsements heavily favor Yes (28 boards including McClatchy CA, SoCal News Group, Mercury News/East Bay Times).
4. Yes campaigns with 2:1 spending often overperform.
5. PPIC's LV screen can overstate Democratic/progressive turnout? Actually PPIC's LV model.

But the strongest evidence is the final-ish poll at 46-50 with only 4% undecided, plus the forecast giving No a slight edge.

Let me check the pollingforecast.com article and possibly other forecasters for base rates. Also check if there are any results out (e.g., is the election over in this scenario? The current date seems Nov 2). Let me do one more check on late-breaking polls and see if there's anything from Nov 1-3, and check LA Times' editorial (they had "-" in the IGS table).

Let me also verify with another angle: search for "Prop 45" "toss up" or predictions from political analysts (e.g., CalMatters, Politico's predictions).

Voters face 145 ballot questions, and only 25 have a poll
Polls cover a fraction of the statewide questions on the 3 November ballot, and California's wealth tax trails in the two newest.
Polling Forecast
·
2 October 2026
·
5 min read
Written in house from our poll data and our forecast.
Photo: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States, CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:California_State_Capitol_from_Capitol_Mall_-_Sacramento_(26429122855).jpg)
Voters in 39 states will decide 145 statewide ballot questions on 3 November, and only 25 of them have been polled, according to our ballot-measures database. Of the 145, 48 reached the ballot through citizens' petitions. The other 97 were put there by legislatures, are referendums on laws already passed, or are bond issues. Constitutional amendments referred by legislatures are the largest single group, at 76.
California and Colorado have the most questions, 14 each, followed by Louisiana with 10 and Massachusetts with 9. By topic, taxes lead with 26, then elections with 22 and education with 13. Four are about abortion and three about congressional redistricting.
We do not forecast ballot measures. What follows is what the published polls say, and how far polls of this kind have been right before.
California's tax fight
The most-polled question in the country is California's Proposition 40, a one-time tax on the wealth of the state's richest residents. We hold nine polls of it, more than any other measure. Through September most showed it ahead. Berkeley IGS had yes at 48 percent and no at 41 in early August, and PPIC had yes at 52 in early September. SurveyUSA and Mason-Dixon, both ending later that month, had yes ahead by 8 and 10 points.
The two newest polls point the other way. The Manhattan Institute's survey ending 1 October had yes at 35 percent and no at 50. IVC Media's, ending a day later with 2,906 likely voters, had 38 to 42, with 21 percent undecided. Across all nine, yes averages 45 percent and no 43. One poll moving would be within normal scatter. Two in a row from different firms, both with no ahead, is a pattern to watch, though the undecided share in the newest is the largest of any poll of the measure.
Two other initiatives would limit new state taxes. EdSource reported that Propositions 41 and 42 are largely backed by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and would effectively cancel the wealth tax if they pass. PPIC found 51 percent for Proposition 41 and 54 percent for Proposition 42. # Support slips for Prop 40 and Prop 45
**DOWNWARD ARC —** Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects.
Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California, as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure.
But Prop 45 also plunged underwater.
Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.

Voters face 145 ballot questions, and only 25 have a poll
Polls cover a fraction of the statewide questions on the 3 November ballot, and California's wealth tax trails in the two newest.
Polling Forecast
·
2 October 2026
·
5 min read
Written in house from our poll data and our forecast.
Photo: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States, CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:California_State_Capitol_from_Capitol_Mall_-_Sacramento_(26429122855).jpg)
Voters in 39 states will decide 145 statewide ballot questions on 3 November, and only 25 of them have been polled, according to our ballot-measures database. Of the 145, 48 reached the ballot through citizens' petitions. The other 97 were put there by legislatures, are referendums on laws already passed, or are bond issues. Constitutional amendments referred by legislatures are the largest single group, at 76.
California and Colorado have the most questions, 14 each, followed by Louisiana with 10 and Massachusetts with 9. By topic, taxes lead with 26, then elections with 22 and education with 13. Four are about abortion and three about congressional redistricting.
We do not forecast ballot measures. What follows is what the published polls say, and how far polls of this kind have been right before.
California's tax fight
The most-polled question in the country is California's Proposition 40, a one-time tax on the wealth of the state's richest residents. We hold nine polls of it, more than any other measure. Through September most showed it ahead. Berkeley IGS had yes at 48 percent and no at 41 in early August, and PPIC had yes at 52 in early September. SurveyUSA and Mason-Dixon, both ending later that month, had yes ahead by 8 and 10 points.
The two newest polls point the other way. The Manhattan Institute's survey ending 1 October had yes at 35 percent and no at 50. IVC Media's, ending a day later with 2,906 likely voters, had 38 to 42, with 21 percent undecided. Across all nine, yes averages 45 percent and no 43. One poll moving would be within normal scatter. Two in a row from different firms, both with no ahead, is a pattern to watch, though the undecided share in the newest is the largest of any poll of the measure.
Two other initiatives would limit new state taxes. EdSource reported that Propositions 41 and 42 are largely backed by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and would effectively cancel the wealth tax if they pass. PPIC found 51 percent for Proposition 41 and 54 percent for Proposition 42. It also found 58 percent backing Proposition 3, which makes permanent the top income tax rates on the highest earners, and 55 percent against Proposition 39, which would require voters to show government-issued identification.
Taxes are on the ballot well beyond California. Washington votes on an initiative that would repeal the tax on household income over $1 million and bar state and local income taxes. Colorado has two measures pulling in opposite directions: Amendment 87 would replace the flat income tax with graduated rates, while Proposition 136 would cap income tax rates at 4.4 percent. None of these has a published poll in our database.
Abortion and redistricting
Four measures concern abortion. In Missouri, Amendment 3, put on the ballot by the legislature, would repeal the abortion-rights amendment voters approved in 2024 and allow abortion only in limited cases; it would also bar gender-transition procedures for minors. The one poll we hold, Saint Louis University and YouGov's from August, had 43 percent for and 44 against, with 13 percent undecided. Wikipedia lists an earlier SLU and YouGov poll, from February, with 47 percent for and 40 against.
Nevada's Question 6 is the second vote required on a constitutional right to abortion, which passed with 64.4 percent in 2024, according to Ballotpedia. Noble Predictive Insights had it at 69 percent yes and 22 no in late September. Voters face 145 ballot questions, and only 25 have a poll
Polls cover a fraction of the statewide questions on the 3 November ballot, and California's wealth tax trails in the two newest.
Polling Forecast
·
2 October 2026
·
5 min read
Written in house from our poll data and our forecast.
Photo: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States, CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:California_State_Capitol_from_Capitol_Mall_-_Sacramento_(26429122855).jpg)
Voters in 39 states will decide 145 statewide ballot questions on 3 November, and only 25 of them have been polled, according to our ballot-measures database. Of the 145, 48 reached the ballot through citizens' petitions. The other 97 were put there by legislatures, are referendums on laws already passed, or are bond issues. Constitutional amendments referred by legislatures are the largest single group, at 76.
California and Colorado have the most questions, 14 each, followed by Louisiana with 10 and Massachusetts with 9. By topic, taxes lead with 26, then elections with 22 and education with 13. Four are about abortion and three about congressional redistricting.
We do not forecast ballot measures. What follows is what the published polls say, and how far polls of this kind have been right before.
California's tax fight
The most-polled question in the country is California's Proposition 40, a one-time tax on the wealth of the state's richest residents. We hold nine polls of it, more than any other measure. Through September most showed it ahead. Berkeley IGS had yes at 48 percent and no at 41 in early August, and PPIC had yes at 52 in early September. SurveyUSA and Mason-Dixon, both ending later that month, had yes ahead by 8 and 10 points.
The two newest polls point the other way. The Manhattan Institute's survey ending 1 October had yes at 35 percent and no at 50. IVC Media's, ending a day later with 2,906 likely voters, had 38 to 42, with 21 percent undecided. Across all nine, yes averages 45 percent and no 43. One poll moving would be within normal scatter. Two in a row from different firms, both with no ahead, is a pattern to watch, though the undecided share in the newest is the largest of any poll of the measure.
Two other initiatives would limit new state taxes. EdSource reported that Propositions 41 and 42 are largely backed by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and would effectively cancel the wealth tax if they pass. PPIC found 51 percent for Proposition 41 and 54 percent for Proposition 42. It also found 58 percent backing Proposition 3, which makes permanent the top income tax rates on the highest earners, and 55 percent against Proposition 39, which would require voters to show government-issued identification.
Taxes are on the ballot well beyond California. Washington votes on an initiative that would repeal the tax on household income over $1 million and bar state and local income taxes. Colorado has two measures pulling in opposite directions: Amendment 87 would replace the flat income tax with graduated rates, while Proposition 136 would cap income tax rates at 4.4 percent. None of these has a published poll in our database.
Abortion and redistricting
Four measures concern abortion. In Missouri, Amendment 3, put on the ballot by the legislature, would repeal the abortion-rights amendment voters approved in 2024 and allow abortion only in limited cases; it would also bar gender-transition procedures for minors. The one poll we hold, Saint Louis University and YouGov's from August, had 43 percent for and 44 against, with 13 percent undecided. Wikipedia lists an earlier SLU and YouGov poll, from February, with 47 percent for and 40 against.
Nevada's Question 6 is the second vote required on a constitutional right to abortion, which passed with 64.4 percent in 2024, according to Ballotpedia. Noble Predictive Insights had it at 69 percent yes and 22 no in late September. Now, the money is roughly balanced: Yes ~$38-41M, No ~$31-38M. Notably, the No side got large late contributions ($5.3M late from Campaign for People Over Polluters). So money advantage for Yes is not overwhelming.

Key: PPIC October (most recent reputable poll, using official ballot language, LV): No 50, Yes 46, 4% DK. Probolsky Oct 27 (thin Yes lead, no toplines). Forecast: No 52.3%.

Structural considerations that push toward No:
1. California's electorate in 2026 midterms: heavily Democratic (Becerra +27), and 54% of Democrats oppose, majority of Republicans support. Democratic turnout advantage in a midterm where Democrats are motivated against Trump. This is a meaningful headwind.
2. The measure's support collapsed once the specifics/attacks (data centers, oil, corporate funders, gutting CEQA) landed. Momentum against.
3. Complexity: 41 pages, initiative statute; hard to explain. Undecided voters default to No on complex measures.
4. The "Yes" campaign lacks Democratic elite support: Newsom neutral, Becerra neutral, Wiener neutral, California YIMBY neutral, building trades opposed, state Democratic Party opposed.
5. Historical base rates: California initiative statutes pass at roughly 40%; measures polling below 50% in final polls rarely pass. Also, measures opposed by labor + environmentalists in a Dem year tend to fail.
6. Also: measures that are "status quo" default (No = keep existing law) with attack ads framing them as corporate giveaways.

Structural considerations for Yes:
1. Big business coalition, utilities, homebuilders; strong affordability message that resonates (cost of living top issue for many).
2. Conceptual support for CEQA reform is very high (73% generic).
3. Newspaper endorsements heavily favor Yes (28 boards including McClatchy CA, SoCal News Group, Mercury News/East Bay Times).
4. Yes campaigns with 2:1 spending often overperform.
5. PPIC's LV screen can overstate Democratic/progressive turnout? Actually PPIC's LV model.

But the strongest evidence is the final-ish poll at 46-50 with only 4% undecided, plus the forecast giving No a slight edge.

1. All Haley breaks loose
https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/11/02/all-haley-breaks-loose-01144782
Will McCarthy: It has been 15 years since Occupy Wall Street brought the issue of wealth inequality to the center of political discourse in the United States.
Billionaires and their bottomless resources had a growing influence over the political system, and the concept of the 1% and the 99% became a familiar part of the American political lexicon.
But years later, through three presidential campaigns and countless Bernie Sanders speeches, voters until now have never had the chance to weigh in on the issue in such a direct way as Proposition 40, a one-time tax on California's billionaires.
The issue pits a fractured coalition against an opponent with endless resources, and the polling suggests the measure is running behind.
But will voters, who routinely express a dour view of billionaires , vote to pass the measure simply to stick it to the man?

2. What the voter records of California’s billionaires reveal

Clockwise from top left: Dr. Dre, Tim Cook, Marissa Mayer, Mark Zuckerberg, Beyonce, Jay-Z | Illustration by Claudine Hellmuth/POLITICO (Getty)
**BIG NUMBERS:** The wealth tax appears increasingly unlikely to pass, with polls showing the measure lagging.
But regardless of the outcome of Proposition 40 on Tuesday, the billionaires who rallied to defeat it have never been more prominent in California politics.

Prop 39:** California Donor Table put in a final $50,000 tranche last week to defeat Prop 39, as polling shows the voter ID measure flagging.
Yes on 39, meanwhile, has continued to pull in checks from individual donors, including $25,000 from Silicon Valley venture capitalist **Asha Jadeja** late last week and $10,000 from entrepreneur **Pete Diamandis**.

# California billionaire tax falling short of majority support, poll finds
A proposed tax on billionaires remains short of majority support as Californians begin casting ballots, according to a new Citrin-POLITICO poll.
Likely voters are essentially where they were a month ago, the survey found, with 46% in favor of Proposition 40 and 43% opposed — despite a recent push by backers of the measure, including Sen.
Bernie Sanders, to rally support for the one-time, 5% tax on billionaires’ assets.

The people paying closest attention to California politics believe we’re headed for a tight finish.
A concurrent survey of POLITICO’s audience of key political and policy influencers in the state — including political staffers, lobbyists, policy advisers and others deeply versed in California’s political landscape — found that plugged-in group was markedly more likely to call the measure too close to call: a 40% plurality of influentials said they didn’t know how Prop 40 would finish, compared to just a quarter of likely voters.

**TAKING THE PULSE:** Support for a measure that would roll back elements of the state’s landmark environmental review law is slipping, according to a new poll.
Half of likely voters said they would vote “no” on Proposition 45 if the election had been held on the day they were surveyed, according to a poll the Public Policy Institute of California released on Tuesday night.
Forty-six percent of likely voters said they were a “yes” on the ballot measure, while 4% didn’t know.
A September PPIC poll found that 49% of voters were a yes on Prop 45.
To pass, a majority of votes for the measure will have to be “yes.”
The PPIC interviewed 1,086 likely voters between Oct. 16 and Oct. 22. The organization found that a majority of likely voters in the Los Angeles and Bay Area regions oppose Prop 45, while a majority of voters in the Inland Empire and San Diego regions support it.

# Newsom’s poison-pill problem
**DOUBLE TROUBLE —** If voters approve Proposition 40’s tax on billionaires, it would be a rebuke to **Gavin Newsom**.
But there’s an even worse scenario for the governor: the billionaire-backed Proposition 42 also passes, winning enough votes to wipe out the tax.
Prop 42 — funded by wealth tax opponents like Google co-founder **Sergey Brin** and endorsed by Newsom — contains a poison pill provision that would void Prop 40’s one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets.
If both measures pass, whichever receives the most yes votes goes into effect.
That’s not the likeliest outcome, but also not impossible.
One recent PPIC poll shows Prop 42 passing with 54% of the vote, and Prop 40 eking by with 52%.
...
Some members of Newsom’s orbit acknowledge the potential of both measures passing could be politically explosive, but said it’s not a particularly pressing concern, mainly because they are increasingly certain the billionaires tax will fail.
Private polling from three separate polling firms — FM3, Public Opinion Strategies and Binder Research — have consistently shown the measure hovering in the high 30s or low 40s, well short of the majority it would need to pass.
That is a notable divergence from public polls, which have regularly shown Prop 40 with a slight edge, usually with a plurality that falls short of 50%.
That is a precarious place for a ballot measure in the closing weeks of an election, but a more optimistic view than the opponents’ intern

6. Support slips for Prop 40 and Prop 45 - Politico

# Support slips for Prop 40 and Prop 45
**DOWNWARD ARC —** Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects.
Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California, as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure.
But Prop 45 also plunged underwater.
Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
...

Voters face 145 ballot questions, and only 25 have a poll
Polls cover a fraction of the statewide questions on the 3 November ballot, and California's wealth tax trails in the two newest.

Written in house from our poll data and our forecast.
Photo: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States, CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:California_State_Capitol_from_Capitol_Mall_-_Sacramento_(26429122855).jpg)
Voters in 39 states will decide 145 statewide ballot questions on 3 November, and only 25 of them have been polled, according to our ballot-measures database. Of the 145, 48 reached the ballot through citizens' petitions. The other 97 were put there by legislatures, are referendums on laws already passed, or are bond issues. Constitutional amendments referred by legislatures are the largest single group, at 76.
California and Colorado have the most questions, 14 each, followed by Louisiana with 10 and Massachusetts with 9. By topic, taxes lead with 26, then elections with 22 and education with 13. Four are about abortion and three about congressional redistricting.
We do not forecast ballot measures. What follows is what the published polls say, and how far polls of this kind have been right before.
California's tax fight
The most-polled question in the country is California's Proposition 40, a one-time tax on the wealth of the state's richest residents. We hold nine polls of it, more than any other measure. Through September most showed it ahead. Berkeley IGS had yes at 48 percent and no at 41 in early August, and PPIC had yes at 52 in early September. SurveyUSA and Mason-Dixon, both ending later that month, had yes ahead by 8 and 10 points.
The two newest polls point the other way. The Manhattan Institute's survey ending 1 October had yes at 35 percent and no at 50. IVC Media's, ending a day later with 2,906 likely voters, had 38 to 42, with 21 percent undecided. Across all nine, yes averages 45 percent and no 43. One poll moving would be within normal scatter. Two in a row from different firms, both with no ahead, is a pattern to watch, though the undecided share in the newest is the largest of any poll of the measure.
Two other initiatives would limit new state taxes. EdSource reported that Propositions 41 and 42 are largely backed by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and would effectively cancel the wealth tax if they pass. PPIC found 51 percent for Proposition 41 and 54 percent for Proposition 42. It also found 58 percent backing Proposition 3, which makes permanent the top income tax rates on the highest earners, and 55 percent against Proposition 39, which would require voters to show government-issued identification.
Taxes are on the ballot well beyond California. Washington votes on an initiative that would repeal the tax on household income over $1 million and bar state and local income taxes. Colorado has two measures pulling in opposite directions: Amendment 87 would replace the flat income tax with graduated rates, while Proposition 136 would cap income tax rates at 4.4 percent. None of these has a published poll in our database.
Abortion and redistricting
Four measures concern abortion. In Missouri, Amendment 3, put on the ballot by the legislature, would repeal the abortion-rights amendment voters approved in 2024 and allow abortion only in limited cases; it would also bar gender-transition procedures for minors. The one poll we hold, Saint Louis University and YouGov's from August, had 43 percent for and 44 against, with 13 percent undecided. Wikipedia lists an earlier SLU and YouGov poll, from February, with 47 percent for and 40 against.
Nevada's Question 6 is the second vote required on a constitutional right to abortion, which passed with 64.4 percent in 2024, according to Ballotpedia. Noble Predictive Insights had it at 69 percent yes and 22 no in late September. Missouri's Proposition A is a referendum on the congressional map the legislature passed in 2025. The same SLU poll found 35 percent for it, 32 against and 33 percent unsure. The 2022 map will be used for this year's House elections whatever the result. KCUR reported that if voters reject the measure, the 2022 lines could stay in place until at least 2031. Colorado's Amendment 86 and Maryland's Question 3 also deal with congressional districts.
Massachusetts, polled in full
Massachusetts is the only state where we hold polls of every question, all nine. Several are not close. Question 1, which would bring the legislature and the governor's office under the public records law, had 84 percent yes in the UMass Amherst poll in August and 63 percent in the CommonWealth Beacon and MassINC poll in September. Question 8, which would repeal legal retail sales of recreational marijuana, had between 24 and 33 percent yes in all three polls.
Others show how much measure polls can disagree. On Question 9, where a yes vote keeps the state's 2024 firearms law, MassINC had 70 percent yes and 18 no in September. The University of New Hampshire, polling the same week, had 38 percent yes, 27 no and 35 percent undecided. On Question 3, a single open primary with the top two advancing, yes led by 19 points in August and by 2 to 7 points in the two September polls. Undecided shares of 20 percent or more are common across the state's questions.
How far measure polls can be trusted
Our database holds no past ballot-measure polls with results, so we cannot score them as we score candidate polls. Other analyses give a rough guide. CalMatters examined PPIC surveys of about 80 California measures since 1998 and found that net support fell by an average of about 6.6 points a month as election day approached, with 71 percent of measures losing support. The fall was larger in low-turnout, non-presidential years. Bonds were the exception: their support rose slightly on average.
Individual cases cut both ways. In August 2024, SLU and YouGov had Missouri's abortion-rights amendment at 52 percent yes and 34 no; it passed with about 51.6 percent. In Nevada, Noble Predictive Insights' final 2024 poll had Question 6 at 59 percent yes with 7 percent undecided; it won 64.4 percent.
That record suggests caution about the measures polling near 50 percent. In California these include Proposition 41 at 51 percent and Proposition 45, which would set deadlines for environmental review, at 49. The housing and research bonds, Propositions 1 and 38, each at 55 percent, belong to the one group that has tended to hold its support. With a month to go, most of the 145 questions will be decided with no public poll at all.

# Support slips for Prop 40 and Prop 45
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects.
Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California, as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure.
But Prop 45 also plunged underwater.
Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.

# Support slips for Prop 40 and Prop 45
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects.
Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California, as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure.
But Prop 45 also plunged underwater.
Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.

CalMatters examined PPIC surveys of about 80 California measures since 1998 and found that net support fell by an average of about 6.6 points a month as election day approached, with 71 percent of measures losing support. # Support slips for Prop 40 and Prop 45
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects.
Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California, as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure.
But Prop 45 also plunged underwater.
Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.

California voters decide 14 statewide propositions on November 3, 2026. On Kalshi and Polymarket, traders buy contracts on whether each one passes, and a contract’s price is the market’s chance. This page puts every measure side by side, with each venue’s price, and updates through the day.
For the separate statewide candidate contest on the same ballot, compare the California governor election (https://defirate.com/odds/california-governor/). For national races on the same election calendar, compare 2026 congressional midterm odds (https://defirate.com/odds/2026-midterms/); these proposition markets settle separate ballot questions.
How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

California voters decide 14 statewide propositions on November 3, 2026. On Kalshi and Polymarket, traders buy contracts on whether each one passes, and a contract’s price is the market’s chance. This page puts every measure side by side, with each venue’s price, and updates through the day.
For the separate statewide candidate contest on the same ballot, compare the California governor election (https://defirate.com/odds/california-governor/). For national races on the same election calendar, compare 2026 congressional midterm odds (https://defirate.com/odds/2026-midterms/); these proposition markets settle separate ballot questions.
How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
CON
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.

California CEQA reform through Proposition 45 would change the approval process for housing, water, energy and infrastructure projects from November 2026.
Proposition 45 would add a new chapter to the California Environmental Quality Act, the 1970 law that requires public agencies to study and disclose a project's environmental effects before approving it.
The chapter, titled the "Building an Affordable California Act," applies to nine categories of projects the measure calls essential: housing, water systems, clean energy, medical facilities, fire and police stations, wildfire risk reduction, broadband, education facilities and transportation.
For those projects, and only if the applicant chooses, it replaces CEQA's open-ended timelines with fixed ones, narrows what an environmental review must consider, caps public comment, and restricts what a court can do when a review is challenged.

Prop 45’s final weekend: two polls, two different answers, and a Bay Area that is the measure’s toughest crowd
PPIC’s October survey has the CEQA overhaul trailing 46% to 50% among likely voters, down from a narrow lead in September. A Probolsky Research poll has it narrowly ahead. Probolsky finds the Bay Area the most skeptical region.
November 1, 2026
Top image: The California State Capitol in Sacramento. Photo: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:California_State_Capitol_from_Capitol_Mall_-_Sacramento_(26429122855).jpg)
By Gideon Paley (https://southbaychronicle.com/reporters/#gideon-paley), Real Estate Development Reporter
ANALYSIS | What the late polling shows on the CEQA overhaul
Prop 45 heads into the last weekend before Tuesday’s election as a close race in the polls. The measure would put deadlines on environmental review and lawsuits under the California Environmental Quality Act for housing, water, energy and other projects it defines as essential.
PPIC: behind, and slipping
The Public Policy Institute of California’s October statewide survey, taken Oct. 16-22, found 46% of likely voters would vote yes, 50% no and 4% undecided, according to PPIC (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/). In September the same survey had the measure ahead, 49% to 46%. The October likely-voter sample was 1,086, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points, so the race is within that range.
The partisan split runs the opposite way from many California housing fights. A majority of Republicans support the measure, while 54% of Democrats oppose it, PPIC found. Gov. Gavin Newsom has stayed on the sidelines, The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) reported. PPIC also measured Prop 40 at 46% yes and 52% no.
Housing under construction at San Francisco’s former Upper Yard site in May 2022. Photo: Pi.1415926535 / CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Upper_Yard_housing_construction,_May_2022.jpg)
Probolsky: ahead, barely
A Probolsky Research poll released Oct. 27 points the other way. The firm headlined its findings “Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/2026/10/27/yes-on-prop-45-leads-by-a-thin-margin/).” It has not published full toplines, and it says it has no client in the race. Men back the measure 51% to 36%, while women oppose it 42% to 36%, the firm reported.
Probolsky also found the Bay Area to be the measure’s weakest region. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up,” Probolsky said in its release.
The money
Both sides are spending heavily. Filings with the Fair Political Practices Commission as of Oct. 29 showed about $39.6 million raised for the Yes side and about $36.3 million for the No side. The Chronicle’s analysis of who is funding each side (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/31/analysis-who-is-funding-prop-45-and-why/) breaks down the largest donors.
Transmission lines carry power from the Encina Power Plant in Carlsbad. Prop. 45 would also cover energy and water projects, not only housing. Photo: Chris Hunkeler from Carlsbad, California, USA / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Transmission_Lines_(8550788014).jpg)
What supporters and opponents argue
Supporters say CEQA lawsuits and open-ended reviews have become a main cause of delay and cost for new housing and infrastructure, and that firm deadlines would get projects built faster. Opponents, including environmental and some labor groups, say the measure would weaken a key tool communities use to challenge harmful projects. The Chronicle’s editorial board has recommended a No vote (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/25/editorial-vote-no-on-prop-45/). That editorial is separate from this newsroom’s reporting.
What to watch Tuesday
The two polls together suggest the result could come down to turnout, especially among Democrats who are splitting from their usual allies and among Bay Area voters. Many California mail ballots are counted after Election Day, so a close statewide measure may not be called on election night.

Proposition 45 is forecast as a environment and energy measure whose Yes vote leans to neither party . The forecast gives No 52.3% and Yes 47.8%. PPIC October: 46-50 No. Probolsky Oct 27: Yes leads by thin margin (unpublished toplines, small firm, likely lower quality).

Additional considerations:
- The No side raised $36.3M as of Oct 29, nearly matching Yes at $39.6M. Unusual for a business measure.
- The measure is opposed by the state Democratic Party, environmental groups, and has negative trendlines.
- Midterm election in California 2026 with a heavily Democratic environment (Becerra leads 61-34, Becerra is the Dem gubernatorial nominee). Democratic turnout advantage → Prop 45 is opposed by 54% of Democrats, supported by majority of Republicans. In a Dem-wave midterm, the Democratic-leaning electorate would hurt Prop 45.
- Historically, California ballot measures polling below 50% with undecideds breaking against tend to fail. Also, initiative statutes generally: about 40% pass.
- Notably the trend was sharply negative: 73 → 49 → 46.

But also, there's a counter-consideration: PPIC's ballot-language polls may understate support; and the "Yes" campaign claims internal polling showing 70-80% with explanation. Also the fiscal impact statement mentions "Initial costs... potentially exceeding $100 million annually" which is negative framing. 2. Prop 45 would make major changes to CEQA. But many CEQA reformers don't support it
https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/joegarofoli/article/prop-45-ceqa-california-22486002.php
Some California leaders who have spent years spearheading changes to California's landmark environmental protection law either haven't taken a position on or are opposing Proposition 45, which would take even bigger chunks out of the California Environmental Quality Act, known as CEQA.
...
A 2024 study of CEQA litigation by the Little Hoover Commission found that on average, "litigation adds almost two years to project time frames.
In the face of such lengthy delays, financing can vanish, stopping a project even if it would eventually have survived the CEQA process and been approved."
...

Billionaires and their bottomless resources had a growing influence over the political system, and the concept of the 1% and the 99% became a familiar part of the American political lexicon.

Voters in 39 states will decide 145 statewide ballot questions on 3 November, and only 25 of them have been polled, according to our ballot-measures database. Of the 145, 48 reached the ballot through citizens' petitions. The other 97 were put there by legislatures, are referendums on laws already passed, or are bond issues. Constitutional amendments referred by legislatures are the largest single group, at 76.
California and Colorado have the most questions, 14 each, followed by Louisiana with 10 and Massachusetts with 9. By topic, taxes lead with 26, then elections with 22 and education with 13. Four are about abortion and three about congressional redistricting.
We do not forecast ballot measures. What follows is what the published polls say, and how far polls of this kind have been right before.
California's tax fight
The most-polled question in the country is California's Proposition 40, a one-time tax on the wealth of the state's richest residents. We hold nine polls of it, more than any other measure. Through September most showed it ahead. Berkeley IGS had yes at 48 percent and no at 41 in early August, and PPIC had yes at 52 in early September. SurveyUSA and Mason-Dixon, both ending later that month, had yes ahead by 8 and 10 points.
The two newest polls point the other way. The Manhattan Institute's survey ending 1 October had yes at 35 percent and no at 50. IVC Media's, ending a day later with 2,906 likely voters, had 38 to 42, with 21 percent undecided. Across all nine, yes averages 45 percent and no 43. One poll moving would be within normal scatter. Two in a row from different firms, both with no ahead, is a pattern to watch, though the undecided share in the newest is the largest of any poll of the measure.
Two other initiatives would limit new state taxes. EdSource reported that Propositions 41 and 42 are largely backed by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and would effectively cancel the wealth tax if they pass. PPIC found 51 percent for Proposition 41 and 54 percent for Proposition 42. It also found 58 percent backing Proposition 3, which makes permanent the top income tax rates on the highest earners, and 55 percent against Proposition 39, which would require voters to show government-issued identification.
Taxes are on the ballot well beyond California. Washington votes on an initiative that would repeal the tax on household income over $1 million and bar state and local income taxes. Colorado has two measures pulling in opposite directions: Amendment 87 would replace the flat income tax with graduated rates, while Proposition 136 would cap income tax rates at 4.4 percent. None of these has a published poll in our database.
Abortion and redistricting

In Missouri, Amendment 3, put on the ballot by the legislature, would repeal the abortion-rights amendment voters approved in 2024 and allow abortion only in limited cases; it would also bar gender-transition procedures for minors. # Support slips for Prop 40 and Prop 45
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects.
Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California, as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure.
But Prop 45 also plunged underwater.
Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.

Massachusetts, polled in full
Massachusetts is the only state where we hold polls of every question, all nine. Several are not close. Question 1, which would bring the legislature and the governor's office under the public records law, had 84 percent yes in the UMass Amherst poll in August and 63 percent in the CommonWealth Beacon and MassINC poll in September. Question 8, which would repeal legal retail sales of recreational marijuana, had between 24 and 33 percent yes in all three polls.
Others show how much measure polls can disagree. On Question 9, where a yes vote keeps the state's 2024 firearms law, MassINC had 70 percent yes and 18 no in September. The University of New Hampshire, polling the same week, had 38 percent yes, 27 no and 35 percent undecided. On Question 3, a single open primary with the top two advancing, yes led by 19 points in August and by 2 to 7 points in the two September polls. Undecided shares of 20 percent or more are common across the state's questions.
How far measure polls can be trusted
Our database holds no past ballot-measure polls with results, so we cannot score them as we score candidate polls. Other analyses give a rough guide. CalMatters examined PPIC surveys of about 80 California measures since 1998 and found that net support fell by an average of about 6.6 points a month as election day approached, with 71 percent of measures losing support. The fall was larger in low-turnout, non-presidential years. Bonds were the exception: their support rose slightly on average.
Individual cases cut both ways. In August 2024, SLU and YouGov had Missouri's abortion-rights amendment at 52 percent yes and 34 no; it passed with about 51.6 percent. In Nevada, Noble Predictive Insights' final 2024 poll had Question 6 at 59 percent yes with 7 percent undecided; it won 64.4 percent.
That record suggests caution about the measures polling near 50 percent. In California these include Proposition 41 at 51 percent and Proposition 45, which would set deadlines for environmental review, at 49. That's a strong signal for No, given Prop 45 is already below 50% in the last poll (Oct 16-22) and the trend was downward.

However, one caution: PPIC's Oct poll was already using ballot language, and the decline from July's generic-question 73% is partly an artifact of question wording. The Sept → Oct change (49-46 → 46-50) is the meaningful movement: Yes dropped 3 points, No rose 4.

The forecast: No 52.3% vs Yes 47.8%. Slight edge to No.
